title: The Recovery Pot Explained (a complete guide to muscle recuperation)
summary: NH explains recovery as a pot that holds muscle damage. Its size sets maximum recoverable volume, it drains at a rate set by how fast you recover, and volume, intensity and frequency decide how much goes in, how fast and how often. He argues the goal is to keep the pot near full between medium and maximum recoverable volume, that each muscle has its own pot, that an empty pot wastes gains, and that once-a-week bro splits are therefore ineffective.
claims: NH explains programming through metaphors: the tree of specificity, the holy trinity of volume, intensity and frequency, the lower back as a bridge, and now the recovery pot
Picture all the muscle damage you inflict going into a pot; its size, which varies by individual, is your maximum recoverable volume
The more you progress, the bigger the pot gets and the more work it takes to fill it, which is what eventually slows gains, not an inability to progress
Pots drain at different rates: two lifters can accumulate and tolerate the same damage yet need different times to fully recover
Intensity is how fast you fill the pot; a volume-skewed lifter like NH has a harder time filling it because he cannot just throw intense reps at it
You can fill the pot with low-quality volume: 10 sets of 20 with a non-challenging weight still fatigues you and takes up room without producing much growth
Because the pot is always draining, the goal is to keep it relatively full; outside a powerlifting meet peak you never want it fully empty
Schedule rest days right after the session that fills the pot the most, to give it the most time to drain

Volume below minimum recoverable volume can lead to regression, around medium recoverable volume you may progress or stagnate, and above maximum recoverable volume work is useless and risks injury, regression and overtraining
Always train between medium and maximum recoverable volume for the best gains
There is a pot for every muscle group and for structures like tendons, and pots can feed into one another; training legs also fills the lower back pot with both muscle and structural damage
The body repairs whether or not you trained, so any time the pot is not filled to the desirable level is time spent wasting gains
NH disagrees with deloads meant to fully empty the pot: there is no extra recovery from something already recovered
After crushing the biceps, waiting longer than about 48-72 hours gains nothing because the muscle is already recovered
Bro splits that train a muscle once a week are ineffective because they leave the pot empty most of the week
For the pot, volume is how much you pour, intensity is how fast you pour and frequency is how often you pour; ignore one and the pot is hard to manage
Leaving the pot empty for several days has no hypertrophy benefit, but you do not need to be fully recovered to train; you could train a muscle at 20% recovery and still grow

Rule of thumb: do not let the pot overflow, and fill it with quality tonnage as often as possible in a template with adequate frequency; for example hit the lats lightly one day and destroy them the next
